title: What is a VPC, what is a subnet, and what makes a subnet "public" vs "private" (a route to an Internet Gateway vs none)?
shortTitle: VPC, Subnet, and What Makes a Subnet Public versus Private

s1_definition.profdef: A VPC (Virtual Private Cloud) is a logically isolated virtual network you define inside an AWS Region, with its own IP address range (CIDR block), route tables, and gateways. A subnet is a sub-range of the VPC's CIDR that lives in exactly one Availability Zone and groups resources together. A subnet is public when its associated route table has a route sending internet-bound traffic (0.0.0.0/0) to an Internet Gateway, and it is private when it has no such route — the single routing rule is the entire difference.
s1_definition.analogy: A VPC is National Bank of India's own private office building, walled off from every other tenant, with its own internal address scheme. A subnet is one floor of that building, and each floor sits in exactly one wing (Availability Zone). A floor is "public" if there is a hallway connecting it to the street-facing main entrance (Internet Gateway) so visitors can come and go, and it is "private" if there is no such hallway at all — the only difference between a public floor and a private floor is whether the hallway to the street exists.
s1_definition.oneliner: A VPC is your private network in AWS, a subnet is a slice of it in one Availability Zone, and a subnet is public only if its route table has a route to an Internet Gateway.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A VPC (Virtual Private Cloud) is a logically isolated virtual network you define inside an AWS Region, with its own IP address range (CIDR block), route tables, and gateways. A subnet is a sub-range of the VPC's CIDR that lives in exactly one Availability Zone and groups resources together. A subnet is public when its associated route table has a route sending internet-bound traffic (0.0.0.0/0) to an Internet Gateway, and it is private when it has no such route — the single routing rule is the entire difference.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A VPC is National Bank of India's own private office building, walled off from every other tenant, with its own internal address scheme. A subnet is one floor of that building, and each floor sits in exactly one wing (Availability Zone). A floor is "public" if there is a hallway connecting it to the street-facing main entrance (Internet Gateway) so visitors can come and go, and it is "private" if there is no such hallway at all — the only difference between a public floor and a private floor is whether the hallway to the street exists.

**One line to remember:** A VPC is your private network in AWS, a subnet is a slice of it in one Availability Zone, and a subnet is public only if its route table has a route to an Internet Gateway.

sections.s2_technical:
A VPC is the foundation of networking in AWS. When you create it you choose a CIDR block, for example 10.0.0.0/16, which gives you 65,536 private IP addresses to carve up. Nothing inside the VPC can talk to the internet or to another VPC unless you explicitly add gateways and routes, so a VPC is private and isolated by default — which is exactly what a bank wants as a starting point.

A subnet is a smaller CIDR carved out of the VPC range, such as 10.0.1.0/24 (256 addresses). A subnet lives in exactly one Availability Zone, so to be highly available you create matching subnets in several zones. AWS reserves five addresses in every subnet (the network address, the VPC router, DNS, a future-use address, and the broadcast address), so a /24 gives you 251 usable addresses.

What makes a subnet public or private is purely the route table associated with it. Every subnet is associated with exactly one route table. If that route table contains a route for 0.0.0.0/0 pointing to an Internet Gateway, resources in the subnet with a public IP can send and receive internet traffic — that is a public subnet. If the route table has no 0.0.0.0/0 to an Internet Gateway, the subnet is private; resources there can reach the internet only indirectly, for example outbound through a NAT Gateway, or not at all.

```text
# Public subnet route table
10.0.0.0/16   → local        (internal VPC traffic)
0.0.0.0/0     → igw-0abc123   (internet, both directions) ← makes it PUBLIC

# Private subnet route table
10.0.0.0/16   → local
0.0.0.0/0     → nat-0xyz789   (outbound only, no inbound)  ← keeps it PRIVATE
# or no 0.0.0.0/0 route at all → fully isolated from the internet
```

The typical banking three-tier layout uses public subnets only for internet-facing components such as the load balancer and NAT Gateway, private subnets for the application servers, and separate private subnets for the database. The web and database tiers never get a route to the Internet Gateway, so they can never be reached directly from the internet.

A senior nuance: giving a subnet a public route is necessary but not sufficient for an instance to be reachable — the instance also needs an actual public or Elastic IP, and the Security Group and NACL must allow the traffic. Public versus private is a property of the subnet's routing; whether a specific instance is reachable also depends on its IP and firewalls.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India must expose a web load balancer to customers but keep the application servers and the database completely unreachable from the internet. Mixing them in one network with internet access would expose the database. This is exactly what public and private subnets solve: the load balancer sits in a public subnet with an Internet Gateway route, the app and database sit in private subnets with none.

Problem 2 — The team needs a clear, programmatic way to decide whether a subnet is public, because a misconfigured route could accidentally expose the database. This is exactly why we model the route table and classify the subnet from it.

We will build a `Subnet` that references a `RouteTable`, and a `SubnetClassifier` that declares a subnet public or private based solely on whether a route to an Internet Gateway exists. Classes: `RouteTable`, `Subnet`, `SubnetClassifier`.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a VPC with CIDR 10.0.0.0/16, a load-balancer subnet with a route to an Internet Gateway, and a database subnet with a route only to a NAT Gateway.

Step 1 — The load-balancer subnet 10.0.1.0/24 is created in Availability Zone ap-south-1a and associated with a route table containing a 0.0.0.0/0 route to the Internet Gateway `igw-0abc123`.

Step 2 — The database subnet 10.0.10.0/24 is created in the same zone and associated with a route table whose 0.0.0.0/0 route points to the NAT Gateway, not the Internet Gateway.

Step 3 — The `SubnetClassifier` inspects the load-balancer subnet's default route. It points to an `igw-`, so the classifier declares it PUBLIC — it can send and receive internet traffic.

Step 4 — The classifier inspects the database subnet's default route. It points to a `nat-`, so the classifier declares it PRIVATE with outbound-only access. The database can never be reached directly from the internet, which is the whole point. The demo also computes that a /24 subnet yields 251 usable IPs after AWS reserves five.

```
2026-10-29 00:52:14 [INFO] Load-balancer subnet is: PUBLIC (route to Internet Gateway)
2026-10-29 00:52:14 [INFO] Database subnet is: PRIVATE (outbound via NAT only)
2026-10-29 00:52:14 [INFO] Usable IPs in a /24: 251
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A VPC is a logically isolated virtual network that I define inside an AWS Region, with its own IP address range as a CIDR block, its own route tables, and its own gateways. The important thing is that a VPC is private and isolated by default — nothing inside it can reach the internet or another VPC until I explicitly add a gateway and a route — which is exactly the safe starting point a bank wants. When I create one I pick a CIDR like 10.0.0.0/16, which gives me about sixty-five thousand private addresses to carve up.

A subnet is a smaller slice of that CIDR, such as 10.0.1.0/24, and it lives in exactly one Availability Zone, so for high availability I create matching subnets across several zones. AWS reserves five addresses in every subnet for the network, the router, DNS, a future-use slot, and broadcast, so a slash twenty-four actually gives me two hundred fifty-one usable addresses.

The heart of the question is what makes a subnet public versus private, and the answer is a single routing rule. Every subnet is associated with one route table. If that route table has a route for 0.0.0.0/0 pointing to an Internet Gateway, the subnet is public and resources there with a public IP can send and receive internet traffic. If there is no such route to an Internet Gateway, the subnet is private — resources there reach the internet only indirectly through a NAT Gateway for outbound, or not at all. There is nothing else that distinguishes them; public versus private is purely about whether the route to the Internet Gateway exists.

At National Bank of India I use the standard three-tier layout. The customer-facing load balancer and the NAT Gateway sit in public subnets with an Internet Gateway route, the application servers sit in private subnets whose default route goes to the NAT Gateway for outbound patches only, and the database sits in its own private subnets with no internet route at all, so it can never be reached directly from the internet. One senior point I always add is that a public route is necessary but not sufficient for an instance to actually be reachable — the instance still needs a real public or Elastic IP and the Security Group and NACL must allow the traffic. So public versus private is a property of the subnet's routing, while whether a specific instance is reachable layers the IP and the firewalls on top.
